reason: The rei vindicatio burden was applied by this court, but the selected quote is a quotation from earlier authorities rather than this court's own holding.
The quoted opportunity-to-cure rule comes from Kristley and the provision was Arbitration Act section 31(2), not SRC030 Civil Procedure Code section 31(2).
The court held that no partition action lies where common ownership has ceased, applying section 2 of the Partition Law to dismiss the action.
The court treated proof of ownership and identifiable property as essential to rei vindicatio and refused to let dismissal of the plaintiffs' action become a declaration for the defendant.
The court itself held that a licensee entering with the plaintiff's leave cannot dispute the plaintiff's title, relying on Evidence Ordinance section 116.
The court held on the facts and strict construction of the power of attorney that general clauses did not authorise a gift of the principal's property.
The section 68 rule was this court's holding, but the selected quote is from Robins v Grogan rather than this court's own statement of the rule.
The court applied Civil Procedure Code section 282 and held the fiscal sale could not be set aside after the statutory objection period had passed.
The rule omits the material Land Development Ordinance conditions about spouse survival and the specific six-month periods under section 68(2).
The section 93(2) proposition was applied by this court, but the supporting quote is a quoted holding from Nimalraj rather than this court's own words.
The court's own reasoning treated express grant and prescription as the two possible juridical sources of the asserted servitude and discussed Prevention of Frauds section 2 for the grant route.
The section 187 duty to give reasoned findings was part of the court's basis for affirming a trial de novo, but the quote is from Meera Mohideen.

The quote is from L. Marian and the statement overstates the rule, because a notary need personally know the executant only to serve as proof under section 68, while SRC001-s2 was not the operative provision.
The court held that a plaintiff seeking specific performance conditional on payment must bring the balance purchase money into court when filing the plaint.
The quoted passage is the Court of Appeal's reproduced reasoning and the Supreme Court's actual basis was the pending-appeal effect of section 154A(3) inserted by Act No. 17 of 2022.
The court expressly held that an acknowledgment under section 12 of the Prescription Ordinance need not be made before expiry of the limitation period.
The court held that adding the registered owner after the two-year prescriptive period for the damage action was impermissible and prejudicial.
The quoted laesio enormis formulation is textbook background, while the court held the doctrine unavailable because the plaintiff knew the true value and fraud was not properly pleaded.
The court held that mandatory Debt Recovery Act summary procedure could not be converted into regular procedure by consent or by the court.
The court held that the plaintiff's unproved notarial deed could not establish paper title without section 68 proof or a recorded admission under section 70.
The rule reverses the section 358 logic, because the creditor lost secured status when it failed to comply with the liquidator's notice and was deemed to have surrendered the charge.
The court interpreted the deed as conveying only house H5, the land covered by it, and the road reservation, with the adjacent lots described only for identification.
The quoted sentence is a factual observation within a broader corpus-identification analysis and omits the actual legal qualification that the totality of evidence must be considered.
The extracted rule omits the decisive post-Act No. 19 of 2011 balance-principal holding and wrongly maps Recovery of Loans by Banks section 5A to SRC001.
The court applied section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance and required a defined starting point and credible evidence before accepting prescriptive title.
